chapter_title: Building User Interfaces with React Native Components

screens.title: Building User Interfaces with React Native Components
screens.subtitle: Use JSX, core components, styles, and Flexbox to create native-feeling mobile layouts.

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how React Native maps JavaScript UI descriptions to native elements on Android and iOS. We use JSX, a JavaScript syntax extension, to declare a tree of components such as View, Text, Image, Button, and TextInput. These are not H T M L elements; they map to native UI primitives so your app looks and performs like a native app. You will see a short code sample that demonstrates a minimal app, then learn how styles are written as JavaScript objects, typically with a StyleSheet creator for performance. We will explore layout using Flexbox, which controls how components grow, align, and distribute space. Finally, you will see how basic interactions work: buttons receive an onPress function and TextInput uses onChangeText to update state. By the end you will be able to compose a simple profile card, style it with StyleSheet, center content with Flexbox, and wire a button to a simple alert. Think about a small native card you use daily — this chapter shows how to build that from components and styles.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: React Native uses JSX and a small set of core components mapped to native controls; styling is JavaScript-based and layout relies on Flexbox.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Building User Interfaces
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Building User Interfaces with React Native

You will learn to describe mobile UI with JSX, compose native-mapped components, style using JavaScript objects, and arrange layouts with Flexbox so your app adapts cleanly to different screens.

This chapter prepares you to build a simple, native-feeling profile card and wire basic interactions like button presses and text updates.

Explore Key Topics
JSX
Write UI using JavaScript XML to describe component trees.
Core Components
Use View, Text, Image, Button, and TextInput as the building blocks.
Flexbox & Interaction
Flexbox positions items; props like onPress and onChangeText handle user input.
UI composition
Compose View and Text to form a native layout.
View
A flexible container that maps to native layout primitives on each platform.
Text
Always wrap visible text in the Text component for correct rendering.
StyleSheet
Create immutable style objects to improve readability and performance.
Flex
A single number that controls how a view grows to fill available space.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These four objectives focus your practice on the essentials you need for building React Native interfaces. First, you will understand JSX, the JavaScript XML syntax used to declare component trees; you'll know why it reads like H T M L but targets native components. Second, you will utilize core React Native components such as View, Text, Image, Button, and TextInput, recognizing the mapping to native controls on Android and iOS. Third, you will implement styling using the StyleSheet creator and inline style objects, learning the camelCase property names and the performance benefits of immutable style objects. Fourth, you will begin to use Flexbox to create responsive layouts that center, distribute, and size components across different devices. Each skill includes a small visual mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can check your progress. Practice by building the small profile card in the hands-on activity and confirm you can center content, show an image, and react to a button press. These objectives will make your UIs consistent, performant, and adaptable.

screens.title: React Native Component Model
screens.subtitle: What components are and how they map to native UI

narration.text: React Native exposes a concise set of core components that act as the building blocks for app interfaces. A View is the fundamental container component; it behaves like a layout box and under the hood maps to a ViewGroup on Android and a UIView on iOS. Text renders textual content and maps to native text controls. Image displays bitmap or network resources. Button provides a simple pressable control, and TextInput is the text entry field. This mapping is crucial: you are not writing H T M L, you are composing native elements through JavaScript. Understanding this model helps you reason about performance and platform behavior. For example, wrapping all text in Text components ensures proper font rendering and touch handling. A typical misconception is to think of these components as web tags; instead, treat them as wrappers that forward rendering to platform-native widgets. A concrete example is a card built from a View containing an Image and two Text elements; the Image source can be a local asset or a network URL. Key takeaway: think in component responsibilities — layout, text, image, input, and touch — and pick the right one for each role.

keyIdea.title: Component mapping
keyIdea.text: Use View, Text, Image, Button, and TextInput because they map directly to native UI elements on Android and iOS.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Component Model
Definition

Core components are small, purpose-built primitives that render to native widgets. Treat each component as the correct semantic choice for content and interaction.

View
Container and layout primitive. Maps to ViewGroup or UIView depending on platform.
Text
Used for all visible text. Always wrap strings in a Text component.
Image, Button, TextInput
Image displays images, Button handles simple presses, TextInput collects user text input.
Concrete Example
A profile card composes an Image for the avatar and Text for the name and title, all wrapped inside a View that controls layout. Because these components map to native widgets, the card will behave like a native view on both Android and iOS.
Scenario
Imagine showing a photo, a bold name, and a subtitle. Use Image for the photo, Text for both strings, and a View to align them with Flexbox.
Key Takeaway

Choose the component by role: layout uses View, text uses Text, images use Image, inputs use TextInput, and simple actions use Button or touchables.

screens.title: A Minimal App in JSX
screens.subtitle: Read and understand the standard App.js structure

narration.text: Let's walk through a minimal React Native app to see how JSX and styles work together. The component imports React and core components, defines a default exported function that returns a tree of View and Text components, and defines styles using the StyleSheet creator. Notice the style prop receives a JavaScript object reference, not a C S S class name. The container typically uses flex to fill the screen and alignment properties to center children. This pattern keeps layout deterministic across devices. A common misconception is to expect traditional H T M L styling rules; instead, you will use camelCase property names and objects. In practice, you will put visual rules in StyleSheet for readability and performance but may use inline objects for small, dynamic adjustments. Try changing a font size or background color and observe the emulator update. The concrete example on screen is a complete App. js you can paste into a project and run to confirm your environment. After reading the code, ask yourself which component is responsible for layout and which for visible text. A Minimal App in JSX means an app component returns a jsx tree; styles are javascript objects passed via the style prop and often created with stylesheet.create.. In practical terms, read and understand the standard app.js structure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: JSX structure
keyIdea.text: An App component returns a JSX tree; styles are JavaScript objects passed via the style prop and often created with StyleSheet.create.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Minimal App
Example App.js

import React from 'react';
import { StyleSheet, Text, View } from 'react-native';

export default function App() {
  return (
    <View style={styles.container}>
      <Text style={styles.title}>Hello, Cohortia Learners!</Text>
      <Text>This is our first React Native UI.</Text>
    </View>
  );
}

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  container: {
    flex: 1,
    backgroundColor: '#fff',
    alignItems: 'center',
    justifyContent: 'center',
  },
  title: {
    fontSize: 24,
    fontWeight: 'bold',
    marginBottom: 10,
    color: '#333',
  },
});
Explanation
  • The exported function App returns a JSX tree composed of View and Text components.
  • StyleSheet.create defines style objects referenced by the style prop, not CSS classes.
  • Container uses flex one to fill available space and center children via justifyContent and alignItems.
  • Text is required for any visible string; plain strings outside Text will not render properly.
Common Mistake

Expecting HTML class names or forgetting to wrap strings in Text are frequent issues for newcomers.

screens.title: Styling: StyleSheet.create and Inline Styles
screens.subtitle: How React Native styles differ from web CSS

narration.text: React Native styles look like C S S but are JavaScript objects with camelCased property names. The preferred pattern is to use the StyleSheet. create method which builds immutable style objects and helps with sending styles to the native layer efficiently. For example, properties like backgroundColor and fontSize replace hyphenated web names. Inline styles are allowed and useful for dynamic values, but overusing them can reduce code clarity and the performance benefits offered by StyleSheet. A concrete example is placing layout rules like flex, alignItems, and justifyContent inside a container style and keeping text appearance in a named title style. Beginners sometimes forget to pass numeric values where expected or to convert percentages correctly; remember that measurable values are numbers for sizes and strings for colors. Practice by moving a small set of visual rules into StyleSheet. create, then toggling a single inline style to see the difference. The main takeaway is to prefer structured StyleSheet objects for maintainability and reserve inline styles for dynamic one-off tweaks. Styling: StyleSheet.create and Inline Styles means use stylesheet.create for organized, performant style objects, and use camelcase property names instead of css hyphenation.. In practical terms, how react native styles differ from web css. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Styling rule
keyIdea.text: Use StyleSheet.create for organized, performant style objects, and use camelCase property names instead of CSS hyphenation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Styling
StyleSheet Pattern

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  container: {
    flex: 1,
    flexDirection: 'column',
    justifyContent: 'center',
    alignItems: 'center',
    backgroundColor: '#f0f0f0',
  },
  title: {
    fontSize: 24,
    fontWeight: 'bold',
    color: '#333',
  },
});
Notes & Examples
  • Property names use camelCase: backgroundColor, marginBottom, fontSize.
  • Use numeric values for dimensions and spacing where appropriate; colors are strings.
  • Inline styles are fine for dynamic values, but keep most rules in StyleSheet for clarity.
When to use inline
When a style depends on runtime values such as a computed width or a dynamic color variable, apply an inline object merged with a StyleSheet entry.

screens.title: Text and Image Components
screens.subtitle: Displaying text correctly and loading images safely

narration.text: Text and Image are distinct core components with different rules. All visible strings must be wrapped in Text components to ensure correct rendering and touch behavior. Image accepts a source prop that can reference a local asset using a require call or a network URL object. For example, local assets use a require with the file path, while network images use an object with a uri string. A common mistake is trying to insert a raw string without a Text wrapper or using web image tags. React Native handles image sizing with explicit width and height styles, so provide dimensions or allow style rules to define them. The concrete examples on the screen show both usage forms. Practically, if you need icons with text, combine Image and Text inside a View and control alignment with Flexbox. The takeaway is to treat every visible string and every bitmap resource with the correct component so platform-specific rendering and performance remain predictable. Text and Image Components means wrap text in text components and provide image sources either as local require calls or as uri objects for network images; always size images explicitly.. In practical terms, displaying text correctly and loading images safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Text & Image
keyIdea.text: Wrap text in Text components and provide Image sources either as local require calls or as uri objects for network images; always size images explicitly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Text & Image
Image Examples

// Local image
<Image source={require('./assets/logo.png')} style={{ width: 100, height: 100 }} />

// Network image
<Image source={{ uri: 'https://reactnative.dev/img/tiny_logo.png' }} style={{ width: 50, height: 50 }} />
Text rules
Always wrap strings inside a Text component. Text components support nested styling and are required for accessibility and correct layout. Combine Text and Image inside a View when building composite items like a labeled avatar.
Common Mistake

Using raw strings or web tags like img will not behave as expected in React Native.

screens.title: Buttons and Pressable Controls
screens.subtitle: When to use Button vs TouchableOpacity or Pressable

narration.text: React Native provides a simple Button component that accepts a title and an onPress handler. Button is useful for quick prototypes but has limited styling. When you need custom visuals, icons, or richer press feedback, wrap content inside TouchableOpacity or Pressable. These touchable wrappers allow you to style the inner View and Text freely, include Images, and manage press states. A typical pattern is to put icon and label inside a touchable and animate opacity or change a background color on press. The chapter gives a simple Button example that shows an alert on press; extend that to a custom control when you need more control over appearance. Remember to wire the onPress handler to a function that performs an action, such as showing an alert or updating state. A common misconception is that Button can be styled like a regular view; instead, switch to a touchable container for custom styling. Practice replacing a Button with a TouchableOpacity if you want to add an avatar or an icon beside the text. Buttons and Pressable Controls means use button for simple actions and touchableopacity or pressable for customizable, styled touchable controls that include icons or custom layouts.. In practical terms, when to use button vs touchableopacity or pressable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pressable pattern
keyIdea.text: Use Button for simple actions and TouchableOpacity or Pressable for customizable, styled touchable controls that include icons or custom layouts.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Buttons
Simple Button

<Button title="Press Me" onPress={() => alert('Button Pressed!')} />
Button is straightforward but limited in styling. For richer controls, use touchable primitives.
Custom touchable
Wrap a View with TouchableOpacity or Pressable to include text, images, and custom layouts. These provide full styling control and press feedback hooks.
Pro tip

Use Pressable when you need granular press-state callbacks; use TouchableOpacity for a simple fade effect.

screens.title: TextInput and Controlled Inputs
screens.subtitle: Capture text with onChangeText and controlled state

narration.text: TextInput is the component used to collect user-entered text. The pattern shown in the chapter makes TextInput a controlled component by keeping its value in component state and updating that state via an onChangeText callback. This ensures the input value always matches the state and lets you use the same value elsewhere in the UI. In the provided example a simple name field updates a greeting. Key points: provide a placeholder to help users, set the value prop to the state variable, and implement onChangeText to update that state. A common mistake is setting a value but not providing onChangeText, which prevents the input from updating. Another pitfall is forgetting to import the state hook when needed. Practically, controlled inputs make validation and derived UI easy because the current text is always available in state. Try typing a name and watching the greeting update to see this pattern in action. TextInput and Controlled Inputs means use a state variable as the value of textinput and update it with onchangetext so the input remains controlled and predictable.. In practical terms, capture text with onchangetext and controlled state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Controlled input
keyIdea.text: Use a state variable as the value of TextInput and update it with onChangeText so the input remains controlled and predictable.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › TextInput
Controlled TextInput Example

import React, { useState } from 'react';
import { View, Text, TextInput, Button, StyleSheet } from 'react-native';

export default function App() {
  const [name, setName] = useState('');

  return (
    <View style={styles.container}>
      <Text style={styles.label}>Enter your name:</Text>
      <TextInput
        style={styles.input}
        placeholder="e.g., Jane Doe"
        onChangeText={text => setName(text)}
        value={name}
      />
      <Button title="Greet Me" onPress={() => alert(`Hello, ${name || 'Guest'}!`)} />
      <Text style={styles.greeting}>Your name is: {name}</Text>
    </View>
  );
}
Explanation
  • useState stores the current text value and keeps the input controlled.
  • onChangeText receives the changed text and updates state immediately.
  • value binds the TextInput appearance to the state variable so it stays in sync.
Common Mistake

Setting a value without an onChangeText handler prevents user edits and makes the field appear read-only.

screens.title: Flexbox for Layout
screens.subtitle: Core Flexbox properties and how they control layout

narration.text: Flexbox is the primary layout system in React Native and governs how children are sized and positioned inside a container. The essential properties to master are flex, flexDirection, justifyContent, and alignItems. The flex property is a number that determines how a child grows to fill available space; a container with flex one typically fills its parent. flexDirection sets the main axis: column is the default and arranges items vertically, while row arranges them horizontally. justifyContent distributes children along the main axis and alignItems controls alignment along the cross axis. A common mistake is confusing main and cross axes, especially when you change flexDirection. Visualize the main axis as the direction children flow in and the cross axis as perpendicular to it. Practically, use flex to let an outer container fill the screen, then use justifyContent and alignItems to center internal content. Try changing flexDirection to row and observe how justifyContent and alignItems swap roles for horizontal layouts. This mental map will help you construct responsive mobile layouts. Flexbox for Layout means understand flex, flexdirection, justifycontent, and alignitems to control the main and cross axes for responsive layouts.. In practical terms, core flexbox properties and how they control layout. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Flexbox basics
keyIdea.text: Understand flex, flexDirection, justifyContent, and alignItems to control the main and cross axes for responsive layouts.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Flexbox
Key Properties
  • flex: a number controlling how a view grows to fill space.
  • flexDirection: main axis direction, column or row.
  • justifyContent: distribution along the main axis.
  • alignItems: alignment along the cross axis.
Common Pitfalls
Forgetting flex on the outer container prevents children from filling the screen. Also, mixing main and cross axis expectations leads to alignment surprises when switching flexDirection.
Centering Example

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  container: {
    flex: 1, // fills screen
    flexDirection: 'column',
    justifyContent: 'center', // centers vertically
    alignItems: 'center', // centers horizontally
  },
});
Key Takeaway

Visualize the main axis and cross axis, and use flex on the outer container to let children adapt to available space.

screens.title: Centering and Layout Troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Common mistakes and how to fix them

narration.text: Centering elements is a frequent task and a common source of confusion. The reliable pattern is to ensure the outer container has a flex value so it can expand, then set justifyContent and alignItems to center. If content does not center, first confirm that flex is applied to the correct ancestor — often the root view needs flex one. Another issue is forgetting that flexDirection changes which axis justifyContent controls. When flexDirection is row, justifyContent distributes horizontally and alignItems vertically. When you have nested views, each view can control its own layout, so add flex and alignment properties at the appropriate level. A practical debugging approach is to add temporary background colors to containers to visualize their bounds and confirm which view is not expanding. Also, remember that Text components do not behave like Views: nested Text inherits some styles differently. The final step is to simplify the tree to the minimal set of containers and reapply styles incrementally until the layout is stable. This step-by-step approach removes guesswork and helps you learn which property affects which axis. Centering and Layout Troubleshooting means if centering fails, ensure the outer container uses flex to fill space and remember how flexdirection swaps main and cross axes.. In practical terms, common mistakes and how to fix them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshoot layout
keyIdea.text: If centering fails, ensure the outer container uses flex to fill space and remember how flexDirection swaps main and cross axes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Troubleshooting
Debugging Steps
  1. Confirm the outermost container has flex set so it can expand.
  2. Visualize container bounds with temporary backgroundColor values.
  3. Check flexDirection to know which axis justifyContent controls.
  4. Simplify nested views and reapply styles incrementally.
Example Fix
If children sit at the top, add flex one to the parent container and set justifyContent to center. If centering only horizontally, ensure alignItems is center as well. Small visual checks often reveal the missing flex property.
Pro tip

Use temporary borders or background colors to quickly see which container is restricting layout space.

Starter Code (App.js)

import React from 'react';
import { StyleSheet, Text, View, Image, Button, Alert } from 'react-native';

export default function App() {
  const handleFollowPress = () => {
    Alert.alert('Follow Action', 'You are now following Jane Doe!');
  };

  return (
    <View style={styles.container}>
      {/* Your profile card components go here */}
      {/* Example: <Image source={{ uri: 'https://via.placeholder.com/150' }} style={styles.profileImage} /> */}
      {/* Example: <Text style={styles.name}>Jane Doe</Text> */}
      {/* Example: <Text style={styles.title}>Mobile Developer</Text> */}
      {/* Example: <Button title="Follow" onPress={handleFollowPress} /> */}
    </View>

}
Implementation Steps
  1. Add an Image with a network uri or local asset and style width and height.
  2. Add two Text elements for the name and title and style typography in StyleSheet.
  3. Add a Button wired to the provided handleFollowPress function.
  4. Use flex and alignment styles to center the card in the parent container.
Why it matters

This activity combines components, styles, layout, and interaction into a single, testable UI you can iterate on and reuse as a pattern across screens.

screens.title: Handling Basic User Interactions
screens.subtitle: Wire onPress and onChangeText to update UI

narration.text: User interactions in React Native are handled by passing handler functions as props. For buttons and touchables you use an onPress prop that receives a function to execute when the control is pressed. For text entry, TextInput exposes onChangeText which receives the current text; use it to update component state and reflect the value back through the value prop. This pattern is immediate and predictable: the UI reads from state and writes to state through handlers. A concrete pattern from the chapter shows a TextInput bound to a name state variable and a Button that alerts a greeting using that name. A common misconception is that input components update the DOM automatically; in React Native, controlled inputs require explicit state updates for the displayed value. Use this pattern to implement validation, to derive other UI text, and to keep your component's state as the single source of truth. Finally, when creating custom pressable controls, ensure you provide accessible labels and consistent feedback for users. Handling Basic User Interactions means pass handler functions to onpress and onchangetext and keep the component's value controlled by state for predictable behavior.. In practical terms, wire onpress and onchangetext to update ui. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interaction pattern
keyIdea.text: Pass handler functions to onPress and onChangeText and keep the component's value controlled by state for predictable behavior.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › User Interactions
Interaction Summary
  • onPress runs a function when a button or touchable is activated.
  • onChangeText receives the new input string each time the user types.
  • Keep inputs controlled by binding value to state so UI stays in sync.
Scenario
Use onChangeText to validate input as the user types, and use onPress to submit or navigate. Controlled patterns let you reuse the same value across components, such as showing a live preview of typed text.
